title: RUTACA Airlines 225
summary: RUTACA Airlines Flight 225, a Douglas C-47A with 20 passengers and 4 crew, crashed shortly after takeoff from Ciudad Bolívar on 25 January 2001 on its return leg of a tourist flight from Canaima. Eyewitnesses stated that one engine appeared to be on fire. The aircraft suddenly lost altitude and crashed into a large tree, exploding on impact with debris raining on the Abobo shantytown. All 24 occupants were killed and one person on the ground was killed. The pilot had recently complained of engine trouble requiring emergency landings.
probable_cause: Engine failure and fire on one engine after takeoff, with all 24 occupants killed and one person on the ground.

title: Oklahoma State University men's basketball team plane crash
summary: A King Air carrying an Oklahoma State basketball team and broadcasters crashed near Denver during descent in snow and darkness. The pilot lost electrical power and most cockpit instruments in instrument meteorological conditions. The investigation found the pilot became spatially disoriented and lost control of the aircraft, entering a steep graveyard spiral that was unrecoverable. The co-pilot, though present, lacked King Air type training.
probable_cause: The pilot's spatial disorientation resulting from failure to maintain positive manual control of the airplane with available flight instrumentation. A contributing factor was loss of AC electrical power during instrument meteorological conditions, which disabled most pilot-side instruments including the altimeter, attitude indicator, and horizontal situation indicator.

title: 2001 Antonov An-70 Crash
summary: An-70 prototype UR-NTK took off from Omsk for cold weather testing in Yakutsk. Within seconds of becoming airborne, one Progress D-27 propfan reached over-speed and shut down automatically. The forward propeller stopped but the aft propeller continued turning, producing negative thrust. An RPM sensor failure on another engine caused its automatic shutdown. With only two functioning engines and one producing 11,000 pounds of negative thrust, the crew successfully turned 180 degrees to return to the airport and crash-landed hard in snow and ice within several hundred yards of the runway without extending landing gear.
probable_cause: Disintegration of the oil line leading to the propeller hub pitch mechanism on one Progress D-27 engine, causing the aft propeller to continue rotating while the forward propeller stopped, producing negative thrust. An RPM sensor malfunction caused automatic shutdown of another engine.

title: 2001 Japan Airlines mid-air incident

agencies.name: Aircraft and Railway Accidents Investigation Commission

summary: Japan Airlines Flight 907, a Boeing 747 climbing to 39000 feet, and Flight 958, a DC-10 cruising at 37000 feet, nearly collided on January 31, 2001. A trainee air traffic controller confused the flight numbers and issued Flight 907 a descent order when intending to command Flight 958. Both aircraft received TCAS and ATC instructions; Flight 907 followed ATC descend while Flight 958 followed TCAS descend, keeping them on a collision course. The aircraft passed within 135 meters before crews executed an evasive maneuver. The incident caused serious injuries to nine crew members and 81 passengers aboard Flight 907.
probable_cause: The trainee controller's confusion of flight numbers and failure to properly separate the aircraft, combined with Flight 907's crew prioritizing ATC instructions over TCAS advisories, nearly caused a collision. title: Loganair 670A
summary: A Short 360 cargo aircraft ditched in the Firth of Forth after a complete loss of propeller thrust at 2,200 feet during the initial climb. Investigation revealed that after parking in snow for 17 hours without protective plugs, snow accumulated in the engine intakes undetected. Upon selecting engine anti-ice systems on, both engines flamed out simultaneously. The crew was unable to reach shore and ditched in the water, killing both crew members.
probable_cause: Large volumes of snow accumulation in unprotected engine intakes following an extended parking period in snow conditions, exacerbated by the lack of established procedures for installing intake covers in adverse weather.

factors.evidence: The aircraft landed at Edinburgh Airport, Scotland, at midnight in snow conditions and was then parked heading directly into moderate to strong surface winds for approximately 17 hours.

Because no protecting plugs were put inside the engine intakes, the wind drove a significant amount of snow into the intakes. The intake plugs were not carried as part of the aircraft's onboard equipment and they were not readily available at Edinburgh Airport.

Information concerning freezing weather conditions in the aircraft manufacturer's maintenance manual had not been included in the airline's Short 360 Operations Manual and was therefore not complied with.
The AAIB discovered that large volumes of snow or slush could have accumulated where it would not have been readily visible to the crew during a pre-flight inspection.
Four seconds later the torque indicators for both engines rapidly fell to zero and the aircraft suffered a complete loss of propeller thrust.
On takeoff this snow changed the engine intake air flow, causing both engines to flame out after both engines' anti-ice vanes were simultaneously opened as per the standard operating procedure.
Realising they could not reach shore, the crew prepared for ditching. At an airspeed of 86 knot with a 6.8degree nose up and 3.6degree left wing down attitude the aircraft impacted the water.

events.text: First officer requested clearance and crew taxied to depart from runway 06 at 17:10 local time.
A normal takeoff was followed by normal reduction in power at 1,200 feet amsl.
At 2,200 feet the co-pilot selected the anti-icing systems on while the pilot changed to a new radio frequency.
Four seconds later the torque indicators for both engines rapidly fell to zero and the aircraft suffered complete loss of propeller thrust.
First officer radioed a Mayday call on the Air traffic control frequency; pilot initiated a descent with reduced airspeed of 110 knots while turning right towards the coast.
Realising they could not reach shore, the crew prepared for ditching.
At an airspeed of 86 knots the aircraft impacted the water at the Firth of Forth; the aircraft was found 65 m offshore in a 45 degree nose down attitude.

title: Thai Airways International 114
summary: An explosion originated in the center fuel tank while cabin crew prepared a Boeing 737-400 for boarding at Don Mueang International Airport in Bangkok. summary: De Havilland DHC-6 Twin Otter Flight 1501 took off from Princess Juliana International Airport at 4:00 pm on 24 March 2001 in good weather. During approach to Gustaf III Airport at Saint Barthélemy, while flying above the western slope of La Tourmente Pass, the aircraft banked steeply to the left. It rapidly lost altitude and crashed into a house, killing all 19 people aboard and one elderly man on the ground. Investigation revealed the captain accidentally moved one engine's thrust lever into the beta range, creating severe thrust asymmetry.
probable_cause: Crew error in managing the plane's thrust lever, causing one engine to enter reverse beta range and creating thrust asymmetry that induced steep left bank. This was the first fatal Twin Otter accident where accidental thrust selection caused propeller to enter the beta range.

title: Vladivostok Air 352
summary: Vladivostok Air Flight 352, a Tupolev Tu-154M, crashed near Irkutsk on 4 July 2001 while approaching Irkutsk Airport. During approach, the first officer made erroneous control inputs including a nose-down input that disconnected the autopilot. The aircraft entered an excessive left bank of up to 48 degrees. Both pilots made alternating control inputs attempting recovery, and excessive nose-up input by both pilots induced an aerodynamic stall at insufficient altitude. The aircraft entered a corkscrew and crashed into farmland, killing all 145 aboard.
probable_cause: Russian investigation committee MAK attributed the causes to pilot error. During the approach, the crew made erroneous input on the aircraft's yoke, causing the airspeed to deplete. A series of errors caused the yoke to be excessively pulled, causing the aircraft to enter a corkscrew. The crew tried to recover but failed due to the aircraft's insufficient altitude.

events.text: The flight took off from Yekaterinburg Koltsovo Airport at 19:47 local time and climbed to its cruising altitude of 10,000 m.
While the turn was being carried out by the crew, the bank angle suddenly increased and the first officer made a nose down input of -4 degree and a left bank input into the steering column.
A warning sounded as the first officer's input caused the autopilot to disconnect and the bank angle to increase from 20 degree to 30 degree.
Captain Goncharuk noticed the increasing bank angle and took over the control to correct the situation but the bank angle continued to increase up to 48 degrees.
The crew sensed an increase of the aircraft's vertical rate of descent and put an excessive nose up input into the yoke causing the aircraft to enter an aerodynamic stall at a severe left bank angle.
The aircraft crashed with its belly first near the settlement of Burdakovka, approximately 22 km from Irkutsk, and immediately exploded upon impact, instantly killing all 145 passengers and crew.

title: Rus 9633
summary: An Ilyushin Il-76TD cargo flight crashed on 14 July 2001 a few seconds after takeoff from Chkalovsky Airport near Moscow. The aircraft was loaded 14 tons above its maximum takeoff weight of 191.9 tons due to a weighing error, with the actual weight approximately 204 tons. The pilots did not perform center-of-gravity calculations. During takeoff rotation, the aircraft immediately listed to the left, and at 23 meters altitude the pilots shifted the horizontal stabilizer nose-down at 5.4 degrees to -3.9 degrees, which is forbidden during takeoff. This caused the aircraft to descend, and when the commander pulled back on the elevator, the aircraft could not recover and struck terrain 530 meters past the runway.
probable_cause: Improper weight and balance causing unstable takeoff, compounded by prohibited modulation of horizontal stabilizer during takeoff which dropped the nose and made recovery impossible at low altitude.

summary: Air Transat Flight 236 lost all engine power while flying over the Atlantic Ocean in darkness due to a fuel leak caused by improper maintenance. Captain Robert Piché and First Officer Dirk DeJager successfully glided the aircraft 65 nautical miles to an emergency landing in the Azores, saving all 306 people on board. events.text: Flight 236 took off from Toronto with 293 passengers and 13 crew on board bound for Lisbon, Portugal.

All engine power was lost while the aircraft was gliding over the Atlantic in darkness.

title: ELK Airways 1007
summary: ELK Airways Flight 1007, an Antonov An-28, departed Tallinn Airport at around 18:05 local time for a short domestic flight to Kärdla on Hiiumaa island. To avoid icing conditions present in the area, the crew switched from an instrument approach to a visual approach. At approximately 18:53 local time, the aircraft impacted treetops and crashed into a marshland about 1.5 km south-east of the airport runway.
